keySentence: You only need happy thoughts and fairy dust to fly.

facts.Page story text 1 (draft, teacher check: The three Darling children stood in their nightclothes and looked up at the open window with wide eyes. Peter had explained that flying required two things and two things only — dust and the right kind of thinking. Tinker Bell circled the room crossly and shook her wings until golden dust covered all three children. Michael thought of his toy bear and his mother's goodnight kiss and lifted slowly off the nursery floor. Wendy thought of the stories she loved most and rose to join her brother at the level of the windowsill. John thought of a cricket match he had won and shot straight past both of them toward the open London sky. You only need happy thoughts and fairy dust to fly.
facts.Page story text 2 (draft, teacher check: The Darling children had always assumed that flying was something entirely out of reach for ordinary people. It was the sort of thing that happened in stories — not in a London nursery on a Tuesday night in winter. But Peter Pan had a way of making the impossible feel not only possible but embarrassingly straightforward. He told them the requirements were so simple that most people failed only because they overcomplicated the thing. Tinker Bell's dust handled the physical side and a single genuinely happy thought handled everything else entirely. The hard part, Peter explained, was that most people couldn't find a thought happy enough because they were too worried. But children, he said, still had access to thoughts pure and light enough to lift them off any floor in the world. You only need happy thoughts and fairy dust to fly.
facts.Page story text 3 (draft, teacher check: There is a particular kind of wisdom embedded in Peter Pan's flight instructions that rewards careful consideration. The fairy dust represents the gift of imagination and wonder — something external that opens possibility but cannot alone suffice. The happy thought represents the internal condition necessary to actually make use of that external possibility. Together they suggest that genuine transformation requires both — an enabling gift from outside and a prepared mind inside. Most people receive fairy dust in some form throughout their lives — moments of beauty, kindness, or unexpected grace. But without the corresponding inner state, those gifts pass through us without lifting us anywhere at all. The happy thought is not wishful thinking — it is a specific quality of attention that makes the gift actually land. Children access it more easily than adults because they have not yet learned to be embarrassed by simple happiness. You only need happy thoughts and fairy dust to fly.
